claim: IL-1α and IL-7 secreted from keratinocytes work in tandem to expand the activated population of resident epidermal γδT-cells.
source: We found that IL-1α and IL-7 secreted from keratinocytes work in tandem to expand the activated population of resident epidermal γδT-cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro γδT-cell proliferation assays showing that both IL-1α and IL-7 are required for optimal γδT-cell expansion, as demonstrated in Figure 3D and related experiments.

claim: Activated γδT-cells preferentially stimulate hair follicle stem cell proliferation.
source: A downstream effect of activated γδT-cells is the preferential proliferation of hair follicle stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that conditioned media from activated γδT-cells causes greater proliferation of HFSCs compared to IFE cells (Figure 4D), and that loss of γδT-cells reduces HFSC proliferation more than IFE proliferation (Figure 2E).

claim: IL-1α-dependent stimulation of dermal fibroblasts optimally stimulates epidermal stem cell proliferation.
source: By contrast, IL-1α-dependent stimulation of dermal fibroblasts optimally stimulates epidermal stem cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that conditioned media from IL-1α-activated dermal fibroblasts causes greater proliferation of IFE cells compared to HFSCs (Figure 4B).

claim: Mice deficient in IL-1 receptor type 1 displayed a 2-day delay in wound closure.
source: As we previously observed, IL-1-dependent signaling is crucial for a normal wound-healing response as mice deficient in the interleukin-1 receptor type 1 (IL1R KO) displayed a 2-day delay in wound closure (Lee et al., 2009; Werner and Smola, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by both data from the current study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and citations to previous work (Lee et al., 2009; Werner and Smola, 2001).

claim: The delay in wound-closure kinetics in IL-1R KO mice manifests significantly at day 3 post-wounding.
source: Interestingly, a closer analysis of the delay in wound-closure kinetics reveals a defect that manifests itself significantly at day 3 post-wounding, suggesting a role for IL-1 signaling in the proliferative phase of the wound-healing response (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which displays wound closure kinetics over time.

claim: Interfollicular stem cell proliferation induced by a wound is significantly impaired in the absence of IL-1 signaling.
source: Extending upon this concept, we observed that the interfollicular stem cell proliferation induced by a wound is significantly impaired in the absence of IL-1 signaling (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1A comparing IFE proliferation in WT versus IL1R KO mice.

claim: CD34+ hair follicle stem cells are highly proliferative in hair follicles proximal to the wound.
source: We found that CD34+ HFSCs were highly proliferative (as noted by Ki67+/CD34+ cells) in hair follicles proximal to the wound (Figure 1B), but were relatively quiescent in follicles distal to the wound site (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating Ki67+/CD34+ cells near wounds.

claim: CD34+ hair follicle stem cells are relatively quiescent in follicles distal to the wound site.
source: We found that CD34+ HFSCs were highly proliferative (as noted by Ki67+/CD34+ cells) in hair follicles proximal to the wound (Figure 1B), but were relatively quiescent in follicles distal to the wound site (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing minimal Ki67 staining in distal follicles.

claim: The increase in HFSC proliferation upon wounding is significantly dependent upon IL-1 signaling.
source: Interestingly, this increase in HFSC proliferation was also significantly dependent upon IL-1 signaling. As shown in Figure 1B, there was a substantial decrease in the number of CD34+ HFSCs that were expressing the proliferating antigen Ki67 3 days post-wounding.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1B and 1C showing reduced HFSC proliferation in IL1R KO mice.

claim: There is a quantitative decrease in proliferating HFSCs as early as one day post-wounding in IL1R KO mice.
source: Upon tracking the status of HFSC proliferation over the course of the wound-healing program, we observed that there was a quantitative decrease in proliferating HFSCs as early as one day post-wounding (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1C tracking HFSC proliferation at days 1, 3, and 5 post-wounding.

claim: The decrease in HFSC proliferation in IL1R KO mice perdures throughout the proliferative phase of the wound-healing program.
source: This decrease in HFSC proliferation perdured throughout the proliferative phase of the wound-healing program.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C showing sustained reduction in HFSC proliferation across multiple time points.

claim: The epidermal region proximal to the wound is hyperplastic.
source: As shown in Figure 1D (and Figure 1—figure supplement 5), the epidermal region proximal to the wound is hyperplastic, but this response is diminished in the absence of IL-1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by epidermal thickness measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Epidermal hyperplasia proximal to wounds is diminished in the absence of IL-1 signaling.
source: As shown in Figure 1D (and Figure 1—figure supplement 5), the epidermal region proximal to the wound is hyperplastic, but this response is diminished in the absence of IL-1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1D showing reduced epidermal thickness in IL1R KO mice compared to WT.

claim: The Casp8 cKO mouse model converts the entire skin to a wound-like state.
source: We addressed this constraint by employing a genetic wound-healing model based on the epidermal ablation of caspase-8 (Casp8 cKO) that converts the entire skin to a wound-like state (Lee et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Lee et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010) and by data throughout the manuscript showing wound-like phenotypes in Casp8 cKO skin.

claim: The Casp8 cKO mouse model displays a thicker epidermis compared to the skin of WT mice.
source: Similar to the observations made with excisional wounds, the Casp8 cKO mouse model of wound healing displayed a thicker epidermis compared to the skin of WT mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by histological data and quantification shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Desensitization of cells to IL-1 signaling via removal of the IL-1 receptor significantly reduces epidermal thickening in Casp8 cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, desensitization of the cells to IL-1 signaling (via the removal of the IL-1 receptor) significantly reduced this epidermal thickening.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1E showing reduced epidermal thickness in Casp8/IL1R dKO compared to Casp8 cKO.

claim: IL-1α-mediated induction of keratinocyte proliferation factors from dermal fibroblasts is one mechanism through which epidermal stem cell proliferation is achieved.
source: These results confirm our previous finding that one mechanism through which epidermal stem cell proliferation is achieved is through IL-1α-mediated induction of keratinocyte proliferation factors from dermal fibroblasts (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Lee et al., 2009) and by data in Figure 4A-B showing that activated fibroblasts produce growth factors and stimulate IFE proliferation.

claim: The thickened epidermal phenotype in Casp8 cKO is partly due to enhanced proliferation of Keratin-5+ IFE cells.
source: The thickened epidermal phenotype was partly due to enhanced proliferation of Keratin-5+ IFE cells, which is elevated in the Casp8 cKO skin and reduced in the absence of IL-1 signaling (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1F and quantification in Figure 1G showing increased Ki67+ IFE cells in Casp8 cKO.

claim: The Casp8 cKO skin has more than a two-fold increase in proliferating HFSC when compared to WT skin.
source: The Casp8 cKO skin had more than a two-fold increase in proliferating HFSC when compared to WT skin (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In the absence of IL-1 signaling, the number of proliferating HFSCs in the Casp8 cKO skin decreases by approximately 30%.
source: In the absence of IL-1 signaling, the number of proliferating HFSCs in the Casp8 cKO skin decreased by ~30% (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1H comparing Casp8 cKO to Casp8/IL1R dKO.

claim: There is a substantial increase in Sox9+ HFSCs in wounded skin.
source: These findings were further corroborated upon detecting HFSCs with an antibody recognizing Sox9 (Adam et al., 2015). There was a substantial increase in Sox9 +HFSCs in the wounded skin and this increase was substantially reduced in the absence of the IL-1 receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 and citation to Adam et al., 2015.

claim: The increase in Sox9+ HFSCs in wounded skin is substantially reduced in the absence of the IL-1 receptor.
source: These findings were further corroborated upon detecting HFSCs with an antibody recognizing Sox9 (Adam et al., 2015). There was a substantial increase in Sox9 +HFSCs in the wounded skin and this increase was substantially reduced in the absence of the IL-1 receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 comparing WT, IL1R KO, and γδT-cell KO wounded skin.

claim: Removing IL-1 signaling is not sufficient to reduce the epidermal thickness in Casp8 cKO to WT levels.
source: Despite the significant contributions of IL-1 signaling to the development of the epidermal thickening in the Casp8 cKO line, removing IL-1 signaling was not sufficient to reduce the epidermal thickness to WT levels (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1E showing that Casp8/IL1R dKO epidermis is still thicker than WT.

claim: Other factors, such as leukocyte-derived signals, contribute to stem cell proliferation in a wound microenvironment.
source: This is probably due to the contribution of other factors, such as leukocyte-derived signals that are capable of promoting stem cell proliferation, in a wound microenvironment (Eming et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eming et al., 2007 and by inference from the observation that IL-1 signaling removal does not completely eliminate the wound phenotype.

claim: IL-1α can stimulate epidermal keratinocyte migration.
source: Moreover, it has previously been reported that IL-1α can stimulate epidermal keratinocyte migration (Chen et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 1995.

claim: HFSCs treated with conditioned media from Casp8 cKO epidermis show a >3 fold increase in chemotaxis relative to cells exposed to CM from wild-type epidermis.
source: When treated with conditioned media (CM) from the Casp8 cKO epidermis, primary mouse HFSCs showed a >3 fold increase in chemotaxis relative to cells exposed to CM from wild-type epidermis.
evidence: This is supported by data from the transwell migration assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: HFSCs lacking the IL-1R remain responsive to the chemotactic cue in the Casp8 cKO CM.
source: Interestingly, HFSCs lacking the IL-1R remained responsive to the chemotactic cue in the Casp8 cKO CM.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 showing that IL1R KO HFSCs still migrate in response to Casp8 cKO CM.

claim: Recombinant IL-1 is incapable of inducing the transwell migration of HFSCs.
source: This finding is consistent with the observation that recombinant IL-1 was incapable of inducing the transwell migration of HFSCs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 showing no significant migration with rhIL-1 treatment.

claim: IL-1α is neither necessary nor sufficient to induce HFSC migration.
source: Altogether, this provides evidence that IL-1α is neither necessary nor sufficient to induce HFSC migration.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 showing that IL1R KO HFSCs can migrate and that rhIL-1 alone does not induce migration.

claim: Macrophages and granulocytes are among the earliest inflammatory cells that respond to injury.
source: Among the earliest inflammatory cells that respond to injury are macrophages and granulocytes, which are known to enhance the proliferation of epidermal stem cells (Martin, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin, 1997 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Macrophages and granulocytes are known to enhance the proliferation of epidermal stem cells.
source: Among the earliest inflammatory cells that respond to injury are macrophages and granulocytes, which are known to enhance the proliferation of epidermal stem cells (Martin, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin, 1997.

claim: In the Casp8 cKO skin, the numbers of macrophages and granulocytes are increased.
source: In the Casp8 cKO skin, the numbers of macrophages and granulocytes were increased and a marked reduction in the numbers of these cells was observed in the absence of IL-1 signaling (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A showing Mac1+ and Gr-1+ cells.

claim: A marked reduction in the numbers of macrophages and granulocytes is observed in Casp8 cKO skin in the absence of IL-1 signaling.
source: In the Casp8 cKO skin, the numbers of macrophages and granulocytes were increased and a marked reduction in the numbers of these cells was observed in the absence of IL-1 signaling (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A comparing Casp8 cKO to Casp8/IL1R dKO.

claim: Following a stress signal such as wounding, γδT-cells become activated and promote epidermal stem cell proliferation by secreting keratinocyte growth factor (KGF, also known as FGF7).
source: Similarly, other well-established contributors to the wound-healing program are epidermal resident γδT-cells, also known as dendritic epidermal T-cells (DETCs). Following a stress signal such as wounding, γδT-cells become activated and promote epidermal stem cell proliferation by secreting keratinocyte growth factor (KGF, also known as FGF7) (Jameson and Havran, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jameson and Havran, 2007 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Wound healing is impaired in γδT-cell deficient mice.
source: Wound healing is impaired in γδT-cell deficient mice, which underscores the important role of these immune cells in the repair process (Jameson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jameson et al., 2002.

claim: γδT-cells play an important role in the recruitment of other immune cells such as macrophages during wound healing.
source: Furthermore, γδT-cells play an important role in the recruitment of other immune cells such as macrophages during wound healing (Jameson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jameson et al., 2005.

claim: In the Casp8 cKO/Tcrd−/− mouse, the number of granulocytes and macrophages are decreased.
source: In the Casp8 cKO/Tcrd−/− (γδT-cell KO) mouse, the number of granulocytes and macrophages were decreased (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A showing reduced Mac1+ and Gr-1+ cells in Casp8/γδTCR dKO.

claim: The impairment of immune cell recruitment in Casp8 cKO/Tcrd−/− mice is similar to the effect observed upon removal of IL-1 signaling in the Casp8 cKO.
source: This impairment of immune cell recruitment is similar to the effect observed upon removal of IL-1 signaling in the Casp8 cKO (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A across different genotypes.

claim: γδT-cell numbers are increased in the Casp8 cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, γδT-cell numbers are increased in the Casp8 cKO mice (Lee et al., 2009), but in the absence of IL-1 signaling, there is a dramatic reduction of the numbers of these cells in the skin (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B and citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: In the absence of IL-1 signaling, there is a dramatic reduction of γδT-cell numbers in Casp8 cKO skin.
source: Interestingly, γδT-cell numbers are increased in the Casp8 cKO mice (Lee et al., 2009), but in the absence of IL-1 signaling, there is a dramatic reduction of the numbers of these cells in the skin (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification in Figure 2B comparing Casp8 cKO to Casp8/IL1R dKO.

claim: The epidermal thickness in the Casp8 cKO/Tcrd−/− mouse is significantly reduced in comparison to that in the Casp8 cKO mouse.
source: We found that the epidermal thickness in the Casp8 cKO/Tcrd−/− mouse was significantly reduced in comparison to that in the Casp8 cKO mouse (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data and quantification in Figure 2C.

claim: The Casp8 cKO skin exhibits robust EdU signal in the bulge region.
source: In the wild-type skin, there is a minimal amount of EdU, whereas the Casp8 cKO skin exhibits robust EdU signal in the bulge region (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Elevated HFSC proliferation in Casp8 cKO skin is markedly reduced in the absence of functional γδT-cells.
source: However, this elevated proliferation is markedly reduced in the Casp8 cKO skin lacking functional γδT-cells.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling data in Figure 2D and quantification in Figure 2E comparing Casp8 cKO to Casp8/Tcrd−/− dKO.

claim: The impact of γδT-cell activity is more pronounced upon HFSC proliferation than in IFE cells in the Casp8 cKO skin.
source: Interestingly, the impact of γδT-cell activity is more pronounced upon HFSC proliferation than in IFE cells in the Casp8 cKO skin (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2E showing differential effects on IFE versus HFSC proliferation.

claim: The reliance on γδT-cell activity for optimized stem cell proliferation is also observed when the stimulus is an excisional wound.
source: This same reliance on γδT-cells activity for optimized stem cell proliferation was also observed when the stimulus was an excisional wound (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3 showing reduced stem cell proliferation in γδT-cell KO wounded mice.

claim: Impairment of epithelial stem cell proliferation resulting from compromised γδT-cells drastically reduces the epidermal hyperplasia that accompanies the wound-healing program.
source: Likewise, the impairment of epithelial stem cell proliferation in the skin resulting from compromised γδT-cells drastically reduces the epidermal hyperplasia that accompanies the wound-healing program (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by epidermal thickness measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The amount of extracellular IL-1α is comparable in Casp8 cKO skin and Casp8 cKO/Tcrd−/− skin.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5, the amount of extracellular IL-1α was comparable in Casp8 cKO skin and Casp8 cKO/Tcrd−/− skin.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: IL-1α levels in wounded wild-type and Tcrd−/− skin are not significantly different.
source: This was verified by quantitation of IL-1 secretion in wounded samples from wild-type and Tcrd−/− skin, wherein the IL-1α levels were not significantly different (Figure 2—figure supplements 6–7).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6 and immunofluorescence in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Despite normal levels of IL-1α in the wound, active γδT-cells are necessary to elicit the early stimulation of HFSC proliferation.
source: These data point to the fact that, despite normal levels of IL-1α in the wound, active γδT-cells are necessary to elicit the early stimulation of HFSC proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IL-1α levels are normal in γδT-cell KO mice but HFSC proliferation is still reduced.

claim: IL-1 signaling converges upon γδT-cells to mediate epithelial stem cell proliferation in the skin.
source: Altogether, these observations suggest that IL-1 signaling converges upon γδT-cells to mediate epithelial stem cell proliferation in the skin.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing that both IL-1 and γδT-cells are required for optimal stem cell proliferation.

claim: The effector function of γδT-cells depends on a combination of a yet unknown antigen recognized by the γδ-TCR and a variety of co-stimulatory molecules.
source: Unlike αβ T-cells, which recognize protein fragments processed by antigen presenting cells, the effector function of γδT-cells depends on a combination of a yet unknown antigen recognized by the γδ-TCR and a variety of co-stimulatory molecules (Witherden et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Witherden et al., 2010 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Keratinocytes that are stressed during wound healing increase the expression of the coxsakie and adenovirus receptor (CAR).
source: In particular, keratinocytes that are stressed during wound healing increase the expression of the coxsakie and adenovirus receptor (CAR), which acts as a co-stimulatory ligand that is recognized by the junctional adhesion molecule-like protein (JAML) on the surface of γδT-cells (Witherden et al., 2010, Witherden and Havran, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Witherden et al., 2010 and Witherden and Havran, 2011.

claim: CAR acts as a co-stimulatory ligand that is recognized by JAML on the surface of γδT-cells.
source: In particular, keratinocytes that are stressed during wound healing increase the expression of the coxsakie and adenovirus receptor (CAR), which acts as a co-stimulatory ligand that is recognized by the junctional adhesion molecule-like protein (JAML) on the surface of γδT-cells (Witherden et al., 2010, Witherden and Havran, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Witherden et al., 2010 and Witherden and Havran, 2011.

claim: Upon activation by a wound, γδT-cells undergo a variety of changes including loss of dendritic extensions, increased proliferation and secretion of cytokines and growth factors.
source: Upon activation by a wound, γδT-cells undergo a variety of changes that are hallmarks of an activated cell, including the loss of dendritic extensions, increased proliferation and secretion of cytokines and growth factors that are essential for wound healing (Jameson and Havran, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jameson and Havran, 2007 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Among the functional consequences of γδT-cell activation is enhanced proliferation of epidermal stem cells.
source: Among the functional consequences of γδT-cell activation is enhanced proliferation of epidermal stem cells (Jameson et al., 2002) and, as shown in Figure 2E, a stronger effect on HFSC proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jameson et al., 2002 and data in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of proliferating γδT-cells is increased three-fold in the Casp8 cKO skin compared to WT controls.
source: We assayed γδT-cell proliferation and found that the number of proliferating γδT-cells was increased three-fold in the Casp8 cKO skin compared to WT controls, whereas a significant decrease was observed in the absence of IL-1 signaling (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3A.

claim: A significant decrease in proliferating γδT-cells is observed in Casp8 cKO skin in the absence of IL-1 signaling.
source: We assayed γδT-cell proliferation and found that the number of proliferating γδT-cells was increased three-fold in the Casp8 cKO skin compared to WT controls, whereas a significant decrease was observed in the absence of IL-1 signaling (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3A comparing Casp8 cKO to Casp8/IL1R dKO.

claim: In excisional wounds, elevated γδT-cell proliferation is dependent on IL-1 signaling.
source: Similarly, in excisional wounds, elevated γδT-cell proliferation is dependent on IL-1 signaling (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: γδT-cells in the caspase-8/IL1R dKO still display increased proliferation compared to wild-type cells.
source: It is noteworthy, however, that γδT-cells in the caspase-8/IL1R dKO still displayed increased proliferation compared to wild-type cells, which may reflect the redundancy in this system.
evidence: This is inferred from data in Figure 3A showing that Casp8/IL1R dKO γδT-cell proliferation is still higher than WT.

claim: Increased γδT-cell activation is observed in the caspase-8 cKO mice, as observed by TNFα expression.
source: We also observed increased γδT-cell activation in the caspase-8/IL1R dKO mice, as observed by TNFα expression (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B and quantification in Figure 3C.

claim: The frequency of activated γδT-cells is markedly reduced in the absence of IL-1 signaling.
source: The frequency of these activated γδT-cells was markedly reduced in the absence of IL-1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3C comparing Casp8 cKO to Casp8/IL1R dKO.

claim: In the newborn thymus, IL-1 signaling has a synergistic effect with IL-7 in enhancing the proliferation of γδT-cells.
source: In the newborn thymus, IL-1 signaling has been shown to have a synergistic effect with IL-7 in enhancing the proliferation of γδT-cells (Lynch and Shevach, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lynch and Shevach, 1992.

claim: Epidermal keratinocytes constitutively express IL-7.
source: Epidermal keratinocytes constitutively express IL-7 and this expression is required for γδT-cell development (Jameson and Havran, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jameson and Havran, 2007 and represents established knowledge.

claim: IL-7 expression is required for γδT-cell development.
source: Epidermal keratinocytes constitutively express IL-7 and this expression is required for γδT-cell development (Jameson and Havran, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jameson and Havran, 2007.

claim: In the Casp8 cKO, IL-7 expression is upregulated.
source: In the Casp8 cKO, IL-7 expression is upregulated and this is not affected by the absence of IL-1 signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: IL-7 upregulation in Casp8 cKO is not affected by the absence of IL-1 signaling.
source: In the Casp8 cKO, IL-7 expression is upregulated and this is not affected by the absence of IL-1 signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 showing no significant difference between Casp8 cKO and Casp8/IL1R dKO.

claim: IL-7 expression is not affected in Casp8 cKO skin or excisional wounds that lack γδT-cells.
source: Similarly, IL-7 expression is not affected in Casp8 cKO skin or excisional wounds that lack γδT-cells (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: IL-1α released from keratinocytes in the Casp8 cKO mouse can act synergistically with IL-7 to enhance γδT-cell proliferation.
source: On the basis of this observation, we hypothesized that IL-1α released from the keratinocytes in the Casp8 cKO mouse can act synergistically with IL-7 to enhance γδT-cell proliferation.
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by in vitro data in Figure 3D showing that both IL-1α and IL-7 are required for maximal γδT-cell proliferation.

claim: γδT-cells treated with Casp8 cKO CM show 2.5-fold increased proliferation compared to WT CM treatment.
source: The number of γδT-cells increased 2.5-fold when they were treated with Casp8 cKO CM rather than WT CM (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 3D.

claim: Treating IL1R−/− γδT-cells with Casp8 cKO CM results in significantly reduced proliferation.
source: Conversely, removing IL-1 signaling by treating IL1R−/− γδ T-cells with Casp8 cKO CM resulted in significantly reduced proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 3D.

claim: Blocking IL-7 signaling in the Casp8 cKO CM with an anti-IL-7 inhibitory antibody blocks γδT-cell proliferation.
source: Similarly, blocking IL-7 signaling in the Casp8 cKO CM with an anti-IL-7 inhibitory antibody blocked γδT-cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 3D.

claim: The effect of blocking IL-7 on γδT-cell proliferation is enhanced when both IL-1 and IL-7 signaling are perturbed in tandem.
source: This effect was enhanced when both IL-1 and IL-7 signaling were perturbed in tandem.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 3D showing additive effects of blocking both pathways.

claim: Adding recombinant human IL-1α to WT CM elicits an increase in γδT-cell proliferation comparable to the effect seen with Casp8 cKO CM.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the addition of rhIL-1α to WT CM elicited an increase in γδT-cell proliferation comparable to the effect seen with Casp8 cKO CM.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 3D.

claim: Simply adding recombinant IL-1 and IL-7 to normal growth media is sufficient to reconstitute the γδT-cell proliferation observed in the Casp8 cKO CM.
source: In fact, simply adding recombinant IL-1 and IL-7 to normal growth media is sufficient to reconstitute the γδT-cell proliferation observed in the Casp8 cKO CM (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 3D.

claim: IL-1 and IL-7 signaling, in conjunction with γδT-cell activation, amplifies the proliferation of γδT-cells in response to stresses that alter epidermal homeostasis.
source: Altogether, these results support the model in which IL-1 and IL-7 signaling, in conjunction with γδT-cell activation, amplifies the proliferation of these cells in response to stresses that alter epidermal homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo data showing synergistic effects of IL-1 and IL-7 on γδT-cell proliferation.

claim: The effect of IL-1 signaling on different stem cell pools is mediated through the dichotomous activation of dermal fibroblasts and γδT-cells.
source: The data presented to date and reported previously (Lee et al., 2009) suggest that the effect of IL-1 signaling on different stem cell pools is mediated through the dichotomous activation of dermal fibroblasts and γδT-cells.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing differential effects of fibroblasts and γδT-cells on IFE versus HFSC proliferation, and is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: Treatment with CM from activated dermal fibroblasts causes a dramatic increase in the proliferation of IFE cells.
source: Treatment with CM from activated df caused a dramatic increase in the proliferation of IFE cells and a modest increase in HFSC proliferation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment with CM from activated dermal fibroblasts causes a modest increase in HFSC proliferation.
source: Treatment with CM from activated df caused a dramatic increase in the proliferation of IFE cells and a modest increase in HFSC proliferation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 4B.

claim: In the absence of IL-1 signaling, the proliferation of both IFE cells and HFSCs induced by activated fibroblasts is reduced to control levels.
source: In the absence of IL-1 signaling, however, the proliferation of both IFE cells and HFSCs was reduced to that of control levels (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFE cells preferentially respond to signals from mesenchymal cells.
source: These observations suggest that IFE cells preferentially respond to signals from mesenchymal cells.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that activated fibroblasts have a stronger effect on IFE proliferation than on HFSC proliferation.

claim: In the backskin of WT mice, γδT-cells are found in close association with the HFSC niche.
source: For instance, in the backskin of WT mice, γδT-cells are found in close association with the HFSC niche (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: Dermal fibroblasts are in close apposition to the IFE cells in the basal layer of the epidermis.
source: On the other hand, dermal fibroblasts are in close apposition to the IFE cells in the basal layer of the epidermis, which would be subjected to the highest concentration of pro-proliferation factors secreted by the activated fibroblasts.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of skin anatomy and the spatial relationship between fibroblasts and the epidermis.

claim: Treatment of primary γδT-cell cultures with Casp8 cKO CM results in their activation, as demonstrated by increased expression of FGF7 and TNFα.
source: The treatment of primary γδT-cell cultures with Casp8 cKO CM resulted in their activation, as demonstrated by their increased expression of FGF7 and TNFα (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: Abrogating IL-1 or IL-7 signaling reduces FGF7 and TNFα expression in γδT-cells.
source: Moreover, abrogating IL-1 or IL-7 signaling was able to reduce FGF7 and TNFα expression, whereas rhIL-1α or rhIL-7 was sufficient to induce maximal FGF7 expression.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: rhIL-1α or rhIL-7 is sufficient to induce maximal FGF7 expression in γδT-cells.
source: Moreover, abrogating IL-1 or IL-7 signaling was able to reduce FGF7 and TNFα expression, whereas rhIL-1α or rhIL-7 was sufficient to induce maximal FGF7 expression.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: Exposure of HFSCs to CM from activated γδT-cells causes a significant increase in HFSC proliferation.
source: Exposure of HFSCs to CM from activated γδT-cells caused a significant increase in the proliferation of the HfSC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 4D.

claim: Activated γδT-cells can stimulate IFE cell proliferation, but the numbers of these cells are 40% smaller than those of HFSCs.
source: Although activated γδT-cells can also stimulate IFE cell proliferation, the numbers of these cells were 40% smaller than those of HFSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of IFE and HFSC proliferation data in Figure 4D.

claim: CM from rhIL-1α- or rhIL-7-treated γδT-cells is sufficient to recapitulate the increased proliferation of HFSCs.
source: Similarly, CM from rhIL-1α- or rhIL-7-treated γδT-cells was sufficient to recapitulate the increased proliferation of the HFSCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 4D.

claim: Treatment of both IFE cells and HFSCs with a combination of CM from activated dermal fibroblasts and γδT-cells substantially increases their proliferation rates.
source: Indeed, treatment of both IFE cells and HFSCs with a combination of CM from activated df and γδT-cells substantially increased their proliferation rates (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation data in Figure 4E showing additive effects.

claim: The differential proliferation of IFE cells and HFSCs is probably due to differences in components present in the cytokine cocktail secreted from either dermal fibroblasts or γδT-cells.
source: One probable reason for the differential proliferation of the IFE cells and HFSCs is the difference in components present in the cytokine cocktail secreted from either df or γδT-cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed differential effects and the known secretion of different factors by these cell types.

claim: Both activated dermal fibroblasts and γδT-cells can secrete the mitogenic factor FGF7.
source: For instance, even though both activated df and γδT-cells can secrete the mitogenic factor FGF7, only γδT-cells secrete IL1F8 or IL-36β (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), which were recently shown to cause proliferation of stem cells (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3, and by citation to Yang et al., 2010.

claim: Only γδT-cells secrete IL1F8 or IL-36β.
source: For instance, even though both activated df and γδT-cells can secrete the mitogenic factor FGF7, only γδT-cells secrete IL1F8 or IL-36β (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), which were recently shown to cause proliferation of stem cells (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: IL1F8 and IL-36β were recently shown to cause proliferation of stem cells.
source: For instance, even though both activated df and γδT-cells can secrete the mitogenic factor FGF7, only γδT-cells secrete IL1F8 or IL-36β (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), which were recently shown to cause proliferation of stem cells (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2010.

claim: IL1F8 signals through the IL-36 receptor.
source: IL1F8 signals through the IL-36 receptor and it is possible that HFSCs are more susceptible to the mitogenic effects of this cytokine.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of IL-1 family signaling pathways.

claim: HFSCs may be more susceptible to the mitogenic effects of IL1F8.
source: IL1F8 signals through the IL-36 receptor and it is possible that HFSCs are more susceptible to the mitogenic effects of this cytokine.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the differential effects of γδT-cells on HFSCs versus IFE cells.

claim: IL-1-mediated activation of γδT-cells preferentially promotes HFSC proliferation.
source: On the basis of these observations, we conclude that IL-1-mediated activation of γδT-cells preferentially promotes HFSC proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing that γδT-cells have a stronger effect on HFSC proliferation than on IFE proliferation.

claim: The downregulation of epidermal caspase-8 is a normal phenomenon upon wounding of the mouse skin.
source: Our previous work has demonstrated that the downregulation of epidermal caspase-8 is a normal phenomenon upon wounding of the mouse skin (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: The conditional ablation of epidermal caspase-8 recapitulates many of the cardinal features of a cutaneous wound-healing response.
source: Moreover, we demonstrated that the conditional ablation of epidermal caspase-8 was able to recapitulate many of the cardinal features of a cutaneous wound-healing response.
evidence: This is supported by data throughout the manuscript showing wound-like phenotypes in Casp8 cKO mice.

claim: IL1α is released immediately upon wounding, downstream of reduction of caspase-8 expression.
source: IL1α is released immediately upon wounding, downstream of reduction of caspase-8 expression (Lee et al., 2009), and mediates the activation of dermal fibroblasts which then stimulate epidermal stem cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009 and by the model shown in Figure 5.

claim: IL-1α mediates the activation of dermal fibroblasts which then stimulate epidermal stem cells.
source: IL1α is released immediately upon wounding, downstream of reduction of caspase-8 expression (Lee et al., 2009), and mediates the activation of dermal fibroblasts which then stimulate epidermal stem cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A-B and the model in Figure 5.

claim: IL-1 signaling can partner with IL-7 to expand the population of active γδT-cells.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that IL-1 signaling can partner with IL-7 (which is constitutively secreted from epidermal keratinocytes) to expand the population of active γδT-cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 showing synergistic effects of IL-1 and IL-7 on γδT-cell proliferation.

claim: Activated γδT-cells can stimulate the proliferation of stem cells within the bulge of the hair follicle.
source: These activated γδT-cells can then stimulate the proliferation of stem cells within the bulge of the hair follicle and can mobilize them for epidermal wound repair.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 4 showing that γδT-cells promote HFSC proliferation.

claim: Activated γδT-cells can mobilize hair follicle stem cells for epidermal wound repair.
source: These activated γδT-cells can then stimulate the proliferation of stem cells within the bulge of the hair follicle and can mobilize them for epidermal wound repair.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing increased HFSC proliferation near wounds and the known role of HFSCs in wound repair.

claim: As the wound-healing response progresses, other infiltrating cells can contribute to or take over the duties of stimulating epithelial stem cell proliferation.
source: As the wound-healing response progresses, given the redundancy of the system, it is likely that other infiltrating cells can contribute to (or take over the duties of) stimulating epithelial stem cell proliferation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known complexity and redundancy of the wound-healing response.

claim: Wounded keratinocytes can produce CCL2 to attract macrophages to a wound.
source: Interestingly, wounded keratinocytes can also produce CCL2 to attract macrophages to a wound (Osaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Osaka et al., 2007.

claim: Activated macrophages secrete IL-1β to induce hair regrowth.
source: These activated macrophages in turn secrete IL-1β (a more potent relative of IL-1α) to induce hair regrowth, and it is tempting to postulate that this mechanism maintains and potentiates the effects of IL-1 +IL-7/γδTcells on HFSC proliferation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning connecting known macrophage functions with the observed effects on HFSC proliferation.

claim: IL-1β is a more potent relative of IL-1α.
source: These activated macrophages in turn secrete IL-1β (a more potent relative of IL-1α) to induce hair regrowth, and it is tempting to postulate that this mechanism maintains and potentiates the effects of IL-1 +IL-7/γδTcells on HFSC proliferation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of IL-1 family cytokines.

claim: Blocking IL-1Receptor-1-dependent signaling does not completely impair the wound repair process.
source: Despite the pleiotropic effects of IL-1 signaling in various cell types and its important function during wound healing, blocking IL-1Receptor-1-dependent signaling does not completely impair the repair process.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing that IL1R KO mice still heal wounds, albeit with a delay.

claim: Compensatory mechanisms involving other IL-1 family members can partially account for the incomplete impairment of wound repair when IL-1R1 signaling is blocked.
source: This can be attributed in part to compensatory mechanisms involving other IL-1 family members.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on knowledge of the IL-1 family and the observed partial phenotype.

claim: Transgenic mice overexpressing IL-1F6 in the basal layer of the epidermis develop severe cutaneous inflammation, hyperkeratosis and acanthosis.
source: Moreover, transgenic mice overexpressing IL-1F6 in the basal layer of the epidermis develop severe cutaneous inflammation, hyperkeratosis and acanthosis (Blumberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blumberg et al., 2007.

claim: Activated γδT-cells release IL-1F8, which has the ability to promote the proliferation of stem cells.
source: Recently, work by Yang et al. showed that activated γδT-cells released IL-1F8, which had the ability to promote the proliferation of stem cells (Blumberg et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blumberg et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2010.

claim: IL-1F6 and IL-1F8 signal through the IL-36 receptor.
source: As IL-1F6 and IL-1F8 signal through the IL-36 receptor and are able to induce the production of mitogenic factors, it is likely that abrogating IL-1R1 signaling alone may not be sufficient to block the epidermal hyperproliferation observed in the Casp8 cKO skin (Towne et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Towne et al., 2004 and represents established knowledge.

claim: IL-1F6 and IL-1F8 are able to induce the production of mitogenic factors.
source: As IL-1F6 and IL-1F8 signal through the IL-36 receptor and are able to induce the production of mitogenic factors, it is likely that abrogating IL-1R1 signaling alone may not be sufficient to block the epidermal hyperproliferation observed in the Casp8 cKO skin (Towne et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Towne et al., 2004.

claim: Abrogating IL-1R1 signaling alone may not be sufficient to block the epidermal hyperproliferation observed in the Casp8 cKO skin.
source: As IL-1F6 and IL-1F8 signal through the IL-36 receptor and are able to induce the production of mitogenic factors, it is likely that abrogating IL-1R1 signaling alone may not be sufficient to block the epidermal hyperproliferation observed in the Casp8 cKO skin (Towne et al., 2004).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known redundancy of IL-1 family signaling and the observation that IL-1R1 deletion does not completely eliminate the phenotype.

claim: In a system as complex as the wound-healing program, removal of an individual component such as IL-1 signaling will impede the kinetics of the process rather than completely inhibit it.
source: Moreover, in a system as complex as the wound-healing program, removal of an individual component such as IL-1 signaling (Kovalenko et al., 2009) will impede the kinetics of the process rather than completely inhibit it (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing delayed but not absent wound closure in IL1R KO mice, and by citation to Kovalenko et al., 2009.

claim: γδT-cells have been found to stimulate hair neogenesis in wounds via Fgf9.
source: It is worth noting that γδT-cells have been found to stimulate hair neogenesis in wounds via Fgf9 (Gay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gay et al., 2013.

claim: Dermal γδT-cells secrete Fgf9 whereas epidermal γδT-cells (DETCs) secrete IL-1F8.
source: Interestingly, it is the dermal γδT-cells that secrete Fgf9 whereas the epidermal pool of γδT-cells (DETCs) secrete IL-1F8, which does not possess hair-neogenesis-promoting properties (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2010.

claim: IL-1F8 does not possess hair-neogenesis-promoting properties.
source: Interestingly, it is the dermal γδT-cells that secrete Fgf9 whereas the epidermal pool of γδT-cells (DETCs) secrete IL-1F8, which does not possess hair-neogenesis-promoting properties (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2010.

claim: There is heterogeneity among cutaneous γδT-cells that can secrete unique repertoires of cytokines with differential effects on the hair follicle.
source: Consequently, it appears that there is heterogeneity among cutaneous γδT-cells that can secrete unique repertoires of cytokines with differential effects on the hair follicle.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dermal and epidermal γδT-cells secrete different factors with different effects.

claim: IL-1 and IL-7 can work together to increase γδT-cell proliferation in the newborn thymus.
source: Consistent with our observations in the skin, IL-1 and IL-7 can also work together to increase γδT-cell proliferation in the newborn thymus, where these cells compete with γδT-cells for survival (Lynch and Shevach, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lynch and Shevach, 1992.

claim: In the case of injury, the synergistic interaction between IL-1 and IL-7 is most probably a response to seal the wound quickly.
source: In the case of injury, this synergistic interaction is most probably a response to seal the wound quickly.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed effects and the known importance of rapid wound closure.

claim: In the presence of a wound-like state, the potentiation of γδT-cell proliferation may be a means to increase the pools of cutaneous epithelial stem cells.
source: Our findings suggest that in the presence of a wound-like state, the potentiation of γδT-cellproliferation may be a means to increase the pools of cutaneous epithelial stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing that γδT-cell expansion leads to increased stem cell proliferation.

claim: Optimal activation of γδT-cells is required for proliferation in hair follicle progenitors and efficient sealing of wounds.
source: Our results are consistent with those of Keyes et al., 2016, which showed that optimal activation of γδT-cells is required for proliferation in hair follicle progenitors and efficient sealing of wounds (Keyes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keyes et al., 2016.

claim: The age-related decline in wound healing correlates with documented changes in the IL-1 family of cytokines that occur with aging.
source: Our results provide a mechanistic basis for their observation and it is interesting to note that the age-related decline that they found in wounding correlates with the documented changes in the IL-1 family of cytokines that occur with aging (Ye et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ye et al., 2002 and represents inference connecting age-related changes in IL-1 to wound healing defects.

claim: The truncated lifespan of the Casp8 cKO mouse is up to approximately 20 days.
source: Unfortunately, the truncated lifespan of the Casp8 cKO mouse (up to ~20 days) and the chronic inflammatory phenotype prevent an investigation of this possibility.
evidence: This is based on observation of the Casp8 cKO mouse model.

claim: The location of the proliferation-inducing cell may impact which stem-cell pool it affects.
source: Furthermore, the location of the proliferating inducing cell may impact which stem-cell pool it affects.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the spatial relationships between different cell types in the skin.

claim: Signals classically associated with immune cells are involved in regulating stem-cell homeostasis.
source: There is an emerging paradigm that signals classically associated with immune cells are involved in regulating stem-cell homeostasis (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015 and represents an emerging concept in the field.

claim: The increased proliferation observed in the Casp8 cKO can be attained through reciprocal keratinocyte–fibroblast or keratinocyte–γδT-cell interactions.
source: We showed that the increased proliferation observed in the Casp8 cKO can be attained through reciprocal keratinocyte–fibroblast or keratinocyte–γδT-cell interactions.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing that both fibroblasts and γδT-cells can promote stem cell proliferation.

claim: The keratinocyte–fibroblast-mediated proliferation is akin to the interaction between the tumor cell and stromal cells.
source: The keratinocyte–fibroblast-mediated proliferation is akin to the interaction between the tumor cell and stromal cells (McAllister and Weinberg, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McAllister and Weinberg, 2010 and represents an analogy to cancer biology.

claim: The activation of γδT-cells promotes tumorigenesis.
source: With regards to the keratinocytes–γδT-cell interaction, it has recently been shown that the activation of γδT-cells promotes tumorigenesis (Arwert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arwert et al., 2010.

claim: Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying stem cell proliferation in a wound microenvironment holds promise for shedding light on complex signaling pathways that mediate tumor initiation.
source: Thus an understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the proliferation of stem cells in a wound microenvironment holds the promise of shedding light on the complex signaling pathways that mediate tumor initiation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential implications of the findings for cancer biology.

claim: Epidermis-specific caspase-8 knockouts were obtained by crossing mice carrying the floxed caspase-8 allele to Krt14-Cre mice.
source: Epidermis-specific knockouts were obtained by crossing mice carrying the floxed caspase-8 allele (Casp8 fl/fl) (Beisner et al., 2005) to Krt14-Cre mice (Vasioukhin et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to generate the mouse model, supported by citations to Beisner et al., 2005 and Vasioukhin et al., 1999.

claim: IL1R–/– mice were purchased from Jackson Laboratory.
source: IL1R–/– mice were purchased from Jackson Laboratory.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the source of the mice.

claim: All animals used in the study were on a C57BL/6 background.
source: All animals were on a C57BL/6 background.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the genetic background of the mice.
